Reproducing Vu et al. (2024) from dandiset 001084¶

Paper. Vu MT, Brown EH, Wen MJ, Noggle CA, Zhang Z, Monk KJ, Bouabid S, Mroz L, Graham BM, Zhuo Y, Li Y, Otchy TM, Tian L, Davison IG, Boas DA, Howe MW (2024). Targeted micro-fiber arrays for measuring and manipulating localized multi-scale neural dynamics over large, deep brain volumes during behavior. Neuron 112, 909-923. doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2023.12.011. This attempt used the full text of the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC10957316). The supplementary PDF could not be retrieved, so the supplementary figure legends were not read.

Dandiset. DANDI:001084, version 0.241023.2011. The paper cites no DANDI version (its data statement points to Zenodo). This is the only published version, so it is pinned; the draft has the same 180 assets and size.

Code read. The paper's analysis code on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.10272874), which settles several choices the Methods leave open (the 11-frame tone delay, the spline basis, the latency rule, how stimulation times are found), and the conversion code catalystneuro/howe-lab-to-nwb at commit 3c53055.

Outside inputs. One claim (fig4-link-published-results) reads the paper's per-fiber results (glm_spline_results.mat, Zenodo Fig04.zip) to check that the dandiset holds the data behind them. Every other claim uses the dandiset alone.

Random numbers: each section that draws them has its own generator with a fixed seed.

def survey(path):
    f = V.open_nwb(path)
    sub = f["general/subject"]
    row = {"path": path, "subject": V._text(sub["subject_id"][()]), "genotype": V._text(sub["genotype"][()]),
           "sex": V._text(sub["sex"][()]), "session": V._text(f["general/session_id"][()]),
           "start": V._text(f["session_start_time"][()])[:19]}
    series = [k for k in f["acquisition"] if k.startswith("FiberPhotometryResponseSeries")]
    row["channels"] = ",".join(s.replace("FiberPhotometryResponseSeries", "") for s in series)
    g = f["acquisition"][series[0]]
    row["frames"] = g["data"].shape[0]
    row["rate_hz"] = round(float(g["starting_time"].attrs["rate"]), 2)
    row["fibers"] = g["data"].shape[1]
    tab = V.fiber_table(f, series[0])
    row["included"] = int(tab.included.sum())
    row["fiber table columns"] = ",".join(sorted(f["general/FiberPhotometry/FiberPhotometryTable"].keys()))
    ip = f["general/optophysiology"]
    row["indicator"] = ",".join(sorted({V._text(ip[k]["indicator"][()]) for k in ip}))
    ev = V.read_events(f)
    for kind in ("Light", "Tone", "Reward", "Lick"):
        row[kind] = int((ev.event_type == kind).sum())
    row["videos"] = sum("Video" in k for k in f["acquisition"])
    return row


with ThreadPoolExecutor(16) as ex:
    files = pd.DataFrame(list(ex.map(survey, paths)))
files = files.sort_values(["subject", "session"]).reset_index(drop=True)

The 16 subjects in the files match the archive's count. The archive lists the approach as "cell population imaging"; the files hold fiber photometry (one trace per optical fiber) and the movies of the fiber bundle it was extracted from. The subjects map onto the paper's experiments as follows, by genotype, indicator, date and the paper's code:

  • DL18, DL20, DL21, DL23, DL27, DL29, DL30: C57BL/6 with dLight1.3b, one light and tone session each (Figures 4, 5, S4, S6).
  • DL15: dLight1.3b, 46 reward sessions over 8 weeks (Figure 1D).
  • 842: D1-cre with GCaMP7f, 470 and 405 nm interleaved at 18 Hz (Figure 1C, S2D-F).
  • DL31, DL32: dLight1.3b, 470 and 415 nm interleaved at 18 Hz, light and tone (Figure S5E-H).
  • Grid-9: DAT-cre with Ach3.0 and jRGECO1a at 11 Hz (Figure S2C); no claim uses it.
  • Opto2: DAT-cre with rDA3m (rDAm3.0), single-fiber stimulation sessions (Figure 6).
  • Opto4, Opto9: DAT-cre with tdTomato, 13 stimulation sessions each, with face videos: the tdTomato controls of Figure 6 ("26 single-site stimulations across 2 mice").
  • UG21: wild type, 3 stimulation sessions, indicator given as tdTomato. Its 3 sessions and 22 included fibers match the paper's rDAm3.0 mouse without opsin ("0/22 non-stimulated sites for 3 single-site stimulations"), and the paper's code names these sessions as the photoswitching controls of Figure S7A. The indicator in the files is consistent with being a mislabel; the files cannot show which indicator was expressed.

The D1-cre mice of Figure 7 (OptoD1_6, 7, 8, 10 in the paper's code), the freely moving mice of Figure 3, the histology of Figure S1, the CT scans of Figure 2, and the 470/405 nm sessions of Figure S5A-D are not in the dandiset.

def load_salient(mouse):
    f = V.open_nwb(V.SALIENT_SESSIONS[mouse])
    dff, times, tab = V.read_dff(f)
    beh = V.read_behavior(f)
    ev = V.read_events(f)
    fs = 1 / np.median(np.diff(beh["t"]))
    ev["on"] = V.nearest_index(beh["t"], ev.start_time.values)
    ev["off"] = V.nearest_index(beh["t"], ev.stop_time.values)
    return {"mouse": mouse, "sex": V._text(f["general/subject/sex"][()]), "dff_all": dff, "times": times,
            "table": tab, "beh": beh, "events": ev, "fs": fs}

The included fibers number 280, from 4 female and 3 male mice, as in the paper; they are the fibers the paper analysed (its code keeps fibers "in_striatum", and the per-mouse counts equal those of the paper's results file, see fig4-link-published-results). The column describes them as "successfully implanted"; the paper's criterion is a tip within or on the border of the striatum, and the included fibers are labelled Caudoputamen, Nucleus accumbens or Striatum, while 87 Caudoputamen fibers are not included. Fiber traces and behaviour have the same number of samples; the fiber series is stored with a regular rate and the behaviour with timestamps, which differ by at most 25 ms, and every event starts on a behaviour timestamp, so events are placed on frames by their behaviour sample, as the code does. Velocity is in m/s and angular velocity in rad/s, with ranges plausible for a mouse on a ball. Six mice have 18 to 21 presentations of each stimulus; DL18 has 14 light and 44 tone presentations. The paper's code uses only 12 kHz tones and its results file has 14 for DL18; the files do not say which of the 44 tones are 12 kHz. Light presentations last 0.7 to 1.0 s and tones about 1.33 s on the trigger line; the code places the tone 11 frames after its trigger (speaker delay).

In [5]:
# Clock check: decode light against tone from the population response after each onset, with the
# true onsets and with all onsets shifted by +-5 s (labels shifted in time).
TONE_SHIFT = 11  # frames at 30 Hz (paper's code)


def decode_accuracy_fs(dff, onsets, labels, shift, w):
    on = onsets + shift
    ok = (on - w >= 0) & (on + w + 1 <= len(dff))
    on, lab = on[ok], labels[ok]
    feats = np.stack([dff[o:o + w].mean(0) - dff[o - w:o].mean(0) for o in on])
    correct = 0
    for i in range(len(on)):  # leave-one-out nearest centroid on z-scored features
        tr = np.ones(len(on), bool)
        tr[i] = False
        mu, sd = feats[tr].mean(0), feats[tr].std(0) + 1e-9
        z = (feats - mu) / sd
        c0, c1 = z[tr & (lab == 0)].mean(0), z[tr & (lab == 1)].mean(0)
        pred = int(np.sum((z[i] - c1) ** 2) < np.sum((z[i] - c0) ** 2))
        correct += pred == lab[i]
    return correct / len(on), len(on)


def decode_accuracy(dff, onsets, labels, shift):
    return decode_accuracy_fs(dff, onsets, labels, shift, 30)


rows = []
for m, d in S.items():
    ev = d["events"]
    st = ev[ev.event_type.isin(["Light", "Tone"])]
    lab = (st.event_type == "Tone").values.astype(int)
    on = st.on.values + TONE_SHIFT * lab
    row = {"mouse": m}
    for shift in (0, 150, -150):
        acc, n = decode_accuracy(d["dff"], on, lab, shift)
        row[f"shift {shift / 30:+.0f} s"] = round(acc, 2)
    row["presentations"] = n
    row["chance (majority)"] = round(max(lab.mean(), 1 - lab.mean()), 2)
    rows.append(row)
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

With the true onsets the stimulus type is decoded from the fibers' responses well above chance in every mouse, and with onsets shifted by 5 s it falls to about chance (for DL18, whose tones outnumber lights 44 to 14, chance is 0.76). The event table and the fiber traces share one clock, as far as this contrast can show.

def load_two_channel(path):
    f = V.open_nwb(path)
    out = {"path": path, "beh": V.read_behavior(f), "events": V.read_events(f)}
    for color in ("Green", "GreenIsosbestic"):
        dff, times, tab = V.read_dff(f, color)
        out[color] = {"dff": dff[:, tab.included.values], "times": times, "fib": tab[tab.included].reset_index(drop=True),
                      "rate": 1 / np.median(np.diff(times))}
    seg = f["processing/ophys/ImageSegmentation/PlaneSegmentation"]
    out["centroids"] = seg["ROICentroids"][:]
    out["included_mask"] = V.fiber_table(f, "FiberPhotometryResponseSeriesGreen").included.values
    return out


with ThreadPoolExecutor(4) as ex:
    TWO = dict(zip(["842-221123", "842-221118", "DL31", "DL32"], ex.map(load_two_channel, [
        "sub-842/sub-842_ses-221123_ophys.nwb", "sub-842/sub-842_ses-221118_ophys.nwb",
        V.ISOSBESTIC_SESSIONS["DL31"], V.ISOSBESTIC_SESSIONS["DL32"]])))
for k, d in TWO.items():
    g, i = d["Green"], d["GreenIsosbestic"]
    ev = d["events"]

Mouse 842 has 82 fibers per channel, 61 included; the paper's Figure 1C describes a 93-fiber array, and its code for the figure reads this mouse's session of 2022-11-23. Its traces start 180 s into the behaviour clock; no claim aligns them to events. DL31 and DL32 are recorded at 18 Hz with the two wavelengths interleaved (415 nm frames 28 ms before the 470 nm frames), as the Methods describe; the behaviour has one sample per frame pair (8177 for DL31), but its timestamps drift from the regular frame times stored for the series by up to half a second over the session, so the regular rate does not describe the frame times exactly. Events are therefore placed by their behaviour sample index, the frame index the paper's code uses, for both channels. Light and tone are decoded from the 470 nm signals better with these onsets (0.90 and 0.80) than with onsets shifted by 5 s (0.40 to 0.65); with 20 presentations per mouse the contrast is weak, so the alignment of these two sessions is consistent with the data but not shown. The bundle-image ROI centroids give one row per fiber of a channel.

dl15 = files[files.subject == "DL15"].copy()
dl15["date"] = pd.to_datetime(dl15.start.str[:10])
print(dl15[["session", "start", "frames", "rate_hz", "fibers", "included", "Reward", "Lick"]].to_string(index=False))
def load_dl15(path):
    f = V.open_nwb(path)
    dff, times, tab = V.read_dff(f)
    beh = V.read_behavior(f)
    ev = V.read_events(f)
    n = len(beh["t"])
    lick = np.zeros(n, bool)
    for _, e in ev[ev.event_type == "Lick"].iterrows():
        a, b = V.nearest_index(beh["t"], np.array([e.start_time, e.stop_time]))
        lick[a:b] = True
    rew = np.sort(V.nearest_index(beh["t"], ev[ev.event_type == "Reward"].start_time.values))
    nxt = np.r_[rew[1:] - 1, n - 1]
    cons = []
    for a, b in zip(rew, nxt):  # first lick after each reward and before the next (getRewInfo.m)
        k = np.flatnonzero(lick[a + 1:b + 1])
        if len(k):
            cons.append(a + 1 + k[0])
    cons = np.array([c for c in cons if c + 121 <= len(dff)], int)
    x = dff[:, tab.included.values]
    act = np.stack([x[c:c + 121] for c in cons]) if len(cons) else np.zeros((0, 121, x.shape[1]))
    return {"path": path, "start": V._text(f["session_start_time"][()])[:10], "n_rew": len(rew), "act": act,
            "n_cons": len(cons), "head": np.round(dff[:200], 6)}


with ThreadPoolExecutor(10) as ex:
    D15 = list(ex.map(load_dl15, dl15.path))
print("\nSessions with 25 rewards or fewer:", int((dl15.Reward <= 25).sum()), "from", dl15[dl15.Reward <= 25].date.min().date(),

      "from", dl15[dl15.Reward > 25].date.min().date(), "to", dl15[dl15.Reward > 25].date.max().date())
print("Rewards followed by a lick before the next reward (consumption), per session:", [s_["n_cons"] for s_ in D15])

opto_paths = [p for p in paths if any(s in p for s in ("Opto2", "Opto4", "Opto9", "UG21"))]


def load_opto(path):
    f = V.open_nwb(path)
    color = "Red"
    dff, times, tab = V.read_dff(f, color)
    fs = 1 / np.median(np.diff(times))
    stim, n_art = V.stimulated_fiber(dff, fs)
    on, off = V.laser_epochs(dff[:, stim], fs) if stim is not None else (np.array([], int), np.array([], int))
    return {"path": path, "subject": path.split("/")[0][4:], "session": path.split("_ses-")[1].split("_")[0],
            "dff": dff, "fs": fs, "table": tab, "stim": stim, "n_artefact": n_art, "on": on, "off": off}

The files hold no stimulation times and no record of which fiber was stimulated. As in the paper's code (getStimTimes.m), the laser epochs are found where the stimulated fiber's DF/F exceeds 0.4 (laser light leaking into the imaged fiber), here without the code's cross-check against the trigger line, which the files do not hold. In Opto2 and UG21 exactly one fiber carries the artefact in each session, except Opto2 2023-03-20f, where 13 fibers do, among them the midbrain fibers 1 to 5; it is left out as a multi-site or midbrain stimulation. UG21's stimulated fibers are 12, 18 and 24, the numbers of the paper's code folders for this mouse (null_12, null_18, null_24), and the first three Opto2 sessions give fibers 13, 17 and 38, matching the code's stri_13, stri_17 and stri_38 recorded on 2023-03-14. There are 7 to 11 epochs of about 1 s, 30 to 60 s apart, as the Methods state. In the tdTomato mice (Opto4, Opto9) the artefact appears on many fibers at once; the fiber with the largest one is taken as the stimulated fiber, which is not always included. Opto9 has 12 sessions, so the files hold 25 tdTomato stimulations where the paper reports 26.

Salient-stimulus GLM (shared by Figures 4, 5 and S4 to S6)¶

For each of the 7 mice: overall velocity and acceleration from the treadmill; for each fiber the lags of the most positive and most negative significant ITI cross-correlation with each (within 500 ms); the GLM of the Methods on the -1 to 2 s windows; and the null of 10000 refits with random onsets and shuffled labels. The Methods' cross-correlation is used; the code's version, in which negative lags are not shifted, is shown as a variant of the point estimates.

In [10]:
rng_glm = np.random.default_rng(10840)
N_NULL = 10000
t0 = time.time()
G = {}
for m, d in S.items():
    ev = d["events"]
    st = ev[ev.event_type.isin(["Light", "Tone"])].sort_values("start_time")
    lab = (st.event_type == "Tone").values.astype(int)
    on = st.on.values + TONE_SHIFT * lab
    fs = d["fs"]
    vel, acc = V.overall_velocity(d["beh"], fs)
    iti = V.iti_mask(len(vel), st.on.values, st.off.values, int(round(fs)))
    lags = V.loco_lags(d["dff"], vel, acc, iti, 15)
    glm = V.CueGLM(d["dff"], vel, acc, lags, fs)
    mu, regr = glm.fit(on, lab, keep_trials=True)
    null = V.cue_glm_null(glm, lab, N_NULL, rng_glm)
    lo, hi = np.percentile(null, [0.5, 99.5], axis=0)
    lags_code = V.loco_lags(d["dff"], vel, acc, iti, 15, code_indexing=True)
    mu_code, _ = V.CueGLM(d["dff"], vel, acc, lags_code, fs).fit(on, lab)
    G[m] = {"on": on, "lab": lab, "vel": vel, "acc": acc, "lags": lags, "mu": mu, "regr": regr, "lo": lo, "hi": hi,
            "mu_code": mu_code, "glm": glm}
    print(f"{m}: {len(on)} presentations ({(lab == 0).sum()} light, {(lab == 1).sum()} tone), {d['dff'].shape[1]} fibers; "
          f"locomotion regressors per fiber {np.bincount(glm.n_loco, minlength=5).tolist()} (0..4); "
          f"windows with NaN rows {int((~np.isfinite(glm._design(on, lab)[1]).all(1)).sum())}; {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

fig4-link-published-results¶

The dandiset's DF/F traces, fibers and stimulus times are those behind the paper's salient-stimulus analysis, so that its per-fiber responses can be linked to the paper's.

Outside input: the paper's glm_spline_results.mat (Zenodo Fig04.zip), read by range requests.

In [11]:
pub = sio.loadmat(io.BytesIO(V.zenodo_member("Fig04.zip", "Fig04/general_functions/glm_spline_results.mat")),
                  squeeze_me=True, struct_as_record=False)
rows = []
for m, g in G.items():
    p = pub[m]
    dff = S[m]["dff"]
    row = {"mouse": m, "fibers dandiset": dff.shape[1], "fibers paper": p.cue1_roi_mu.shape[1]}
    for c, name in ((0, "light"), (1, "tone")):
        ons = g["on"][g["lab"] == c]
        eta = np.nanmean(V.windows(dff, ons, -30, 60), 0)
        pm = getattr(p, f"cue{c + 1}_roi_mu")
        row[f"{name} trials"] = f"{len(ons)}/{getattr(p, f'cue{c + 1}_loco_regr_act').shape[2]}"
        row[f"{name} raw max|diff|"] = float(np.abs(eta - pm).max()) if eta.shape == pm.shape else np.nan
        row[f"{name} spline r"] = round(np.corrcoef(g["mu"][c].ravel(), getattr(p, f"cue{c + 1}_spline_mu").ravel())[0, 1], 4)
        psig = getattr(p, f"cue{c + 1}_spline_sig")
        up = V.runs_of(g["mu"][c] > g["hi"][c])
        down = V.runs_of(g["mu"][c] < g["lo"][c])
        row[f"{name} sig agree"] = round(float(np.mean((psig[:, 0] == up) & (psig[:, 1] == down))), 3)
    rows.append(row)
link = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(link.to_string(index=False))
agree_all = sum((link[f"{n} sig agree"] * link["fibers dandiset"]).sum() for n in ("light", "tone")) / (2 * link["fibers dandiset"].sum())
print("\nSignificance agreement over all fiber and stimulus pairs:", round(float(agree_all), 3))
print("Spline estimates pooled over mice: light r = %.4f, tone r = %.4f" % (
    np.corrcoef(np.concatenate([G[m]["mu"][0].ravel() for m in G]), np.concatenate([pub[m].cue1_spline_mu.ravel() for m in G]))[0, 1],
    np.corrcoef(np.concatenate([G[m]["mu"][1].ravel() for m in G]), np.concatenate([pub[m].cue2_spline_mu.ravel() for m in G]))[0, 1]))

# DL18: identify the paper's 14 tones (12 kHz) among the 44 by matching its per-trial activity.
p = pub["DL18"]
dff = S["DL18"]["dff"]
tones = G["DL18"]["on"][G["DL18"]["lab"] == 1]
win = V.windows(dff, tones, -30, 60)  # tones x frames x fibers
pt = p.cue2_loco_regr_act  # frames x fibers x trials
match, best_r, second_r = [], [], []
for k in range(pt.shape[2]):
    r = np.array([np.ma.corrcoef(np.ma.masked_invalid(pt[:, :, k].ravel()), np.ma.masked_invalid(w.ravel()))[0, 1] for w in win])
    o = np.argsort(r)[::-1]
    match.append(o[0]); best_r.append(r[o[0]]); second_r.append(r[o[1]])
match = np.array(match)
print("\nDL18 tones matched to the paper's 14 trials:", (match + 1).tolist(), "; distinct:", len(set(match)))
print("match r: min %.3f; best competitor r: max %.3f" % (min(best_r), max(second_r)))
eta14 = np.nanmean(win[match], 0)
print("DL18 raw tone average over the 14 matched tones against the paper's: max |diff| = %.2e" % np.abs(eta14 - p.cue2_roi_mu).max())
DL18_12K = tones[np.sort(match)]

# The GLM and null of DL18 refitted with only these 14 tones, compared with the paper's results
g = G["DL18"]
keep = (g["lab"] == 0) | np.isin(g["on"], DL18_12K)
mu18, _ = g["glm"].fit(g["on"][keep], g["lab"][keep])
null18 = V.cue_glm_null(g["glm"], g["lab"][keep], N_NULL, np.random.default_rng(18))
lo18, hi18 = np.percentile(null18, [0.5, 99.5], axis=0)
up18, down18 = V.runs_of(mu18[1] > hi18[1]), V.runs_of(mu18[1] < lo18[1])
psig = p.cue2_spline_sig
print("DL18 tone with the 14 matched tones: spline r = %.4f (44 tones: %.4f); significance agreement %.3f (44 tones: %.3f)" % (
    np.corrcoef(mu18[1].ravel(), p.cue2_spline_mu.ravel())[0, 1], link.loc[link.mouse == "DL18", "tone spline r"].iloc[0],
    np.mean((psig[:, 0] == up18) & (psig[:, 1] == down18)), link.loc[link.mouse == "DL18", "tone sig agree"].iloc[0]))
n_pairs = 2 * link["fibers dandiset"].sum()
agree_14 = agree_all + (np.mean((psig[:, 0] == up18) & (psig[:, 1] == down18)) - link.loc[link.mouse == "DL18", "tone sig agree"].iloc[0]) \
    * link.loc[link.mouse == "DL18", "fibers dandiset"].iloc[0] / n_pairs
print("Significance agreement over all fiber and stimulus pairs with DL18's 14 tones: %.3f" % agree_14)
print("Pooled tone spline r with DL18's 14 tones: %.4f" % np.corrcoef(
    np.concatenate([(mu18 if m == "DL18" else G[m]["mu"])[1].ravel() for m in G]), np.concatenate([pub[m].cue2_spline_mu.ravel() for m in G]))[0, 1])

Result: reproduced. For every mouse the raw triggered averages computed from the dandiset equal the paper's published ones (largest difference 0.0) for light, and for tone in the six mice other than DL18, whose file holds 44 tones where the paper's results use 14. The GLM spline estimates correlate with the published ones at r = 0.9957 for light and 0.9922 for tone over all fibers, and the significance of increases and decreases agrees for 93.6% of fiber and stimulus pairs (lowest: DL18 tone 0.684, with 44 tones in place of 14; DL29 light 0.822). DL18's 14 tones are identified one to one (match r at least 0.952, best competing tone at most 0.693), and their raw average equals the published one. Refitted with these 14 tones, DL18's tone estimates correlate with the published ones at r = 0.9977 and significance agrees for 0.947 of its fibers; with them, agreement over all pairs is 94.5% and the pooled tone r 0.9974. Per mouse, r is below 0.99 for DL29 light (0.979) and for DL27 and DL29 tone (0.989, 0.986). The dandiset's traces, fiber order and stimulus times are those of the paper's analysis; only the tone frequency of DL18 is missing.

fig4e-light-increases-widespread¶

The light evokes transient increases in dopamine release across many striatal locations.

Paper's p < 1e-6 is 0.01 ** 3, three independent frames outside the 99% band. In the null refits: a frame is outside the band with rate 0.0104, and three given consecutive frames all are with rate 0.0037 (0.01 ** 3 = 1e-6)

Result: reproduced. 240 of 280 fibers (86%) have a significant increase to light and 38 a significant decrease; by the signed largest value, 237 are increases and 11 decreases. Every mouse has increases in most fibers (from 34 of 51 in DL21 to 50 of 53 in DL20), and decreases are concentrated in DL21 (22 of 51) and DL29 (12 of 45). The test's chance rate of a significant increase per fiber, from null refits, is 0.024 (about 7 of 280 fibers), and 0.043 for an increase or a decrease. This is far above the paper's stated p < 1e-6, which is 0.01 cubed: in the null refits three given consecutive frames are all outside the band at a rate of 0.0037, not 1e-6, because neighbouring frames of the spline estimate are correlated, and the test looks for such a run anywhere in the 31 frames. The procedure is the paper's (its published significance calls agree with these for 93.6% of pairs, see fig4-link-published-results), so the difference lies in how the paper states the rate.

fig4e-light-anterior-posterior-gradient¶

Light-evoked dopamine increases follow an amplitude gradient from the anterior striatum into the posterior tail, where increases are less prevalent and smaller.

In [13]:
def light_gradient(w, tail):
    rho, p = stats.spearmanr(w.AP, w.value_light)
    t = w.AP <= tail
    table = [[int((w.up_light & t).sum()), int((~w.up_light & t).sum())],
             [int((w.up_light & ~t).sum()), int((~w.up_light & ~t).sum())]]
    _, p_frac = stats.fisher_exact(table, alternative="less")
    _, p_amp = stats.mannwhitneyu(w.value_light[t], w.value_light[~t], alternative="less")
    return {"tail AP <=": tail, "n tail": int(t.sum()), "rho AP-light": round(rho, 3), "p rho": p,
            "frac up tail": round(table[0][0] / max(t.sum(), 1), 2), "frac up other": round(table[1][0] / (~t).sum(), 2),
            "p frac": p_frac, "median tail": round(w.value_light[t].median(), 4),
            "median other": round(w.value_light[~t].median(), 4), "p amp": p_amp}

Result: partially reproduced. The light value rises from posterior to anterior (Spearman rho = 0.168, p = 0.0047) and is smaller in the tail (median 0.0055 against 0.0117 DF/F, p = 0.0013), but increases are not less prevalent there: 83% of tail fibers against 86% elsewhere have a significant increase (p = 0.38). The same holds with the tail at -0.8 or -1.3 mm and with the code's lags (rho = 0.162). The gradient is carried by DL18, DL20 and DL27 (rho 0.45 to 0.69); three mice have a negative point estimate (DL23 -0.43, DL29 -0.25, DL30 -0.12). Ranked within each mouse and tested by permuting within mice, so that differences between mice cannot drive it, the correlation is r = 0.152 (p = 0.013).

fig4f-tone-tail-increase-anterior-decrease¶

The tone evokes the strongest dopamine increases at sites in the posterior tail, while anterior to the tail it evokes primarily decreases.

In [14]:
def tone_pattern(w, tail, col="value_tone"):
    t = w.AP <= tail
    _, p_amp = stats.mannwhitneyu(w[col][t], w[col][~t], alternative="greater")
    top = w.sort_values(col, ascending=False).head(10)
    ant = w[~t & w.sig_tone]
    n_dec, n_inc = int((ant[col] < 0).sum()), int((ant[col] > 0).sum())
    p_bin = stats.binomtest(n_dec, n_dec + n_inc, 0.5, alternative="greater").pvalue if n_dec + n_inc else np.nan
    return {"tail AP <=": tail, "n tail": int(t.sum()), "median tail": round(w[col][t].median(), 4),
            "median anterior": round(w[col][~t].median(), 4), "p tail>anterior": p_amp,
            "top10 in tail": int((top.AP <= tail).sum()), "anterior sig dec": n_dec, "anterior sig inc": n_inc,
            "p binomial": p_bin}


print(pd.DataFrame([tone_pattern(W, t) for t in (TAIL, -0.8, -1.3)]).to_string(index=False))
print("\nTail fibers with a significant tone increase / decrease:", int((W.is_tail & W.up_tone).sum()), "/", int((W.is_tail & W.down_tone).sum()),
      "of", int(W.is_tail.sum()), "; anterior:", int((~W.is_tail & W.up_tone).sum()), "/", int((~W.is_tail & W.down_tone).sum()), "of", int((~W.is_tail).sum()))

Result: reproduced. Tail fibers have larger tone values than anterior fibers (median 0.0092 against -0.0026 DF/F, p = 5.5e-13), all 10 of the largest tone values are in the tail, and 32 of 35 tail fibers have a significant increase with none decreasing. Anterior to the tail, 103 fibers with a significant tone response decrease and 60 increase (binomial p = 0.00047). The amplitude comparison and the anterior excess of decreases hold at every tail boundary (-0.8, -1.0 and -1.3 mm) and with the code's lags, but at -1.3 mm only 5 of the 10 largest tone values are in the tail, below the 6 that part (a) of the criterion needs. The result is the same with DL18 restricted to its 14 12-kHz tones (108 decreases against 60). The anterior decrease is not uniform across mice: it is significant in DL21 (36 against 3) and DL23 (17 against 6), while DL18, DL20, DL27 and DL30 have as many or more anterior increases.

figs4eh-patterns-not-movement¶

Locomotor changes to the stimuli are variable and bi-directional, while the dopamine release patterns to light and tone are consistent, so the patterns are stimulus and not movement driven.

        for part, mask in (("acc", sign > 0), ("dec", sign < 0)):

            for r in range(dff.shape[1]):
                split.append({"mouse": m, "fiber": r, "stim": name, "part": part, "value": v[r], "value_base": vb[r]})

Result: partially reproduced. Locomotion after the stimuli varies across mice and presentations: the split into presentations followed by acceleration and by deceleration ranges from 0 and 21 (DL29 light) to 21 and 23 (DL18 tone), and the mean velocity change is positive in some mice and negative in others for both stimuli. The fiber maps of the two splits correlate (light r = 0.873 over 235 fibers, tone r = 0.784 over 229), and the light map has positive medians in both splits. The tone pattern holds after acceleration (tail median 0.0073, anterior median -0.0031) but not after deceleration, where the anterior median is positive (0.0042, tail 0.0098). This test uses raw DF/F, as the paper's code (sal_stim_bubbles_loco.m) does, without a baseline and without the locomotion regressors of the GLM. With each split's pre-onset mean subtracted (a variant), the maps correlate at r = 0.755 (light) and 0.823 (tone), and the tone pattern holds in both splits (anterior median -0.0043 after acceleration, -0.0024 after deceleration; tail 0.0069 and 0.0101), which points to the level before onset in the deceleration trials as the cause of the failure under the code's measure.

figs5-isosbestic-no-pattern¶

With isosbestic (415 nm) excitation, large fluorescence changes and spatial patterns to light and tone are not observed, ruling out a hemodynamic origin of the release patterns.

rng_s5 = np.random.default_rng(5415)
rows, S5, NULL5, VAR13 = [], [], [], []
for m in ("DL31", "DL32"):
    d = TWO[m]
    beh, ev = d["beh"], d["events"]
    st = ev[ev.event_type.isin(["Light", "Tone"])].sort_values("start_time")
    for color, label in (("Green", "470"), ("GreenIsosbestic", "415")):
        ch = d[color]
        fs = ch["rate"]
        n_fr = len(ch["dff"])
        b2 = {k: beh[k][:n_fr] for k in ("roll", "pitch", "angular")}  # behaviour sample k = frame pair k
        vel, acc = V.overall_velocity(b2, fs)
        lab = (st.event_type == "Tone").values.astype(int)
        on = V.nearest_index(beh["t"], st.start_time.values) + 6 * lab  # 6-frame tone delay at 18 Hz (code)
        off = V.nearest_index(beh["t"], st.stop_time.values)
        iti = V.iti_mask(len(vel), on - 6 * lab, off, int(round(fs)))
        lags = V.loco_lags(ch["dff"], vel, acc, iti, 9)
        glm = V.CueGLM(ch["dff"], vel, acc, lags, fs)
        mu, _ = glm.fit(on, lab)
        null = V.cue_glm_null(glm, lab, N_NULL, rng_s5)
        lo, hi = np.percentile(null, [0.5, 99.5], axis=0)
        for c, name in ((0, "light"), (1, "tone")):
            up, down = V.runs_of(mu[c] > hi[c]), V.runs_of(mu[c] < lo[c])
            val, sig = V.signed_peak(mu[c], up, down)
            fib = ch["fib"]
            rows.append({"mouse": m, "nm": label, "stim": name, "fibers": len(val), "trials": int((lab == c).sum()),
                         "median |value|": round(float(np.median(np.abs(val))), 4), "significant": int(sig.sum()),
                         "rho AP-value": round(stats.spearmanr(fib.AP, val)[0], 3)})
            S5.append(pd.DataFrame({"mouse": m, "nm": label, "stim": name, "fiber": np.arange(len(val)), "value": val}))
            # reference: |signed largest value| of the null refits (no stimulus), first 1000 refits
            nv = np.where(np.abs(null[:1000, c].min(1)) > np.abs(null[:1000, c].max(1)), null[:1000, c].min(1), null[:1000, c].max(1))
            NULL5.append({"mouse": m, "nm": label, "stim": name, "abs": np.abs(nv).ravel()})
        # variant: 13 spline functions over the 1 s at 18 Hz (the Methods' 13 df), same lags
        glm13 = V.CueGLM(ch["dff"], vel, acc, lags, fs, knot_intervals=10)
        mu13, _ = glm13.fit(on, lab)
        null13 = V.cue_glm_null(glm13, lab, N_NULL, rng_s5)
        lo13, hi13 = np.percentile(null13, [0.5, 99.5], axis=0)
        for c, name in ((0, "light"), (1, "tone")):
            v13, s13 = V.signed_peak(mu13[c], V.runs_of(mu13[c] > hi13[c]), V.runs_of(mu13[c] < lo13[c]))
            VAR13.append({"mouse": m, "nm": label, "stim": name, "abs": np.abs(v13), "sig": int(s13.sum())})

Result: partially reproduced. With 415 nm excitation almost no fiber responds significantly (light 2 against 45 at 470 nm; tone 1 against 18 over 96 fibers of two mice), and the AP correlations seen at 470 nm for tone (-0.49 and -0.43) are not present at 415 nm (-0.19 and 0.16). The median absolute value at 415 nm is 0.49 of that at 470 nm for light, below the criterion's half, but 0.68 for tone. The largest-magnitude value has a floor: with random onsets its median is 0.0025 (470 nm) and 0.0019 DF/F (415 nm). The tone median at 470 nm (0.0027) is only 0.0002 above that floor, so the tone ratio compares two values near the noise and cannot fall to half; for light the 470 nm median is 0.0017 above the floor and the 415 nm median 0.0001. With 13 spline functions over the 1 s, as the Methods state for the main GLM, in place of the code's 9 at 18 Hz, the ratios are 0.55 (light) and 0.70 (tone), with 36 and 15 significant fibers at 470 nm against 1 and 0 at 415 nm. The 470 and 405 nm sessions of Figure S5A-D are not in the dandiset.

Counted as the paper's code counts, one frame later, the means are 220.8, 305.0 and 426.5 ms, within 2 ms of the paper's values, with SDs of 38.1, 98.7 and 196.5 ms against 42.5, 100.0 and 197.1. The difference from the paper is the code's one-frame offset. One tone increase has no half-max crossing before its peak.

fig5g-light-latency-gradient¶

Dopamine release latencies to light follow an anterior-posterior gradient, with faster increases in the anterior striatum, consistent with wave-like dynamics.

In [20]:
def trial_latencies(m, c, kind):
    """Per presentation and fiber, half-max latency (frames) of the trial activity with locomotion
    regressed out, where the fiber's mean response is significant and the trial exceeds the null band
    for 3 consecutive frames (rise_dip_time.m)."""
    g = G[m]
    tau = g["glm"].tau
    w = (tau >= 0) & (tau <= 30)
    act = g["regr"][g["lab"] == c][:, w, :]  # trials x 31 x fibers
    up = V.runs_of(g["mu"][c] > g["hi"][c])
    down = V.runs_of(g["mu"][c] < g["lo"][c])
    out = np.full((act.shape[0], act.shape[2]), np.nan)
    for t in range(act.shape[0]):
        for r in range(act.shape[2]):
            x = act[t, :, r]
            if kind == "increase" and up[r] and V.runs_of(x > g["hi"][c][:, r])[0]:
                out[t, r] = V.half_max_latency(x, 1)
            if kind == "decrease" and down[r] and V.runs_of(x < g["lo"][c][:, r])[0]:
                out[t, r] = V.half_max_latency(x, -1)
    return out


REL = []
for m in G:
    rise_l = trial_latencies(m, 0, "increase")
    rise_t = trial_latencies(m, 1, "increase")
    dip_t = trial_latencies(m, 1, "decrease")
    either_t = np.fmin(rise_t, dip_t)
    for name, mat in (("light rise", rise_l), ("tone either", either_t), ("tone rise", rise_t), ("tone dip", dip_t)):
        rel = mat - np.nanmin(mat, axis=1, keepdims=True)
        for r in range(mat.shape[1]):
            n = int(np.isfinite(rel[:, r]).sum())
            REL.append({"mouse": m, "fiber": r, "measure": name, "n_trials": n,
                        "rel_ms": 1000 * np.nanmean(rel[:, r]) / FS if n else np.nan,
                        "abs_ms": 1000 * np.nanmean(mat[:, r]) / FS if n else np.nan})
REL = pd.DataFrame(REL).merge(W[["mouse", "fiber", "AP", "ML", "DV"]], on=["mouse", "fiber"])


def gradient(measure, sign_word, rng=None):
    d = REL[(REL.measure == measure) & REL.rel_ms.notna()]
    rho, p = stats.spearmanr(d.AP, d.rel_ms)
    print(f"{measure}: fibers with a latency {len(d)} (trials per fiber median {d.n_trials.median():.0f});"
          f" Spearman rho(AP, relative latency) = {rho:.3f}, p = {p:.2g} ({sign_word})")
    if rng is not None:
        r_w, p_w = V.within_group_rank_corr(d.AP, d.rel_ms, d.mouse, 5000, rng)
        print(f"   variant, within mice (ranks within each mouse, permutation within mice): r = {r_w:.3f}, p = {p_w:.2g}")
    for c in ("ML", "DV"):
        r2, p2 = stats.spearmanr(d[c], d.rel_ms)
        print(f"   rho({c}, relative latency) = {r2:.3f}, p = {p2:.2g}")
    return d, rho, p


d_light, rho_l, p_l = gradient("light rise", "negative = anterior faster", np.random.default_rng(5071))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
ax.scatter(d_light.AP, d_light.rel_ms, s=10)
ax.set_xlabel("AP (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("mean relative latency, light (ms)")
plt.show()
print("Plotted ranges: AP %.2f to %.2f; latency %.0f to %.0f ms" % (d_light.AP.min(), d_light.AP.max(), d_light.rel_ms.min(), d_light.rel_ms.max()))

light rise: fibers with a latency 240 (trials per fiber median 18); Spearman rho(AP, relative latency) = -0.285, p = 7e-06 (negative = anterior faster)

   variant, within mice (ranks within each mouse, permutation within mice): r = -0.223, p = 0.0014
   rho(ML, relative latency) = 0.263, p = 3.8e-05
   rho(DV, relative latency) = -0.005, p = 0.93

Plotted ranges: AP -1.96 to 1.45; latency 49 to 442 ms

Result: reproduced. Over the 240 fibers with a light latency, the mean latency relative to the fastest fiber of each presentation is shorter anteriorly (Spearman rho(AP, latency) = -0.285, p = 7e-06). Latency also increases laterally (rho(ML) = 0.263, p = 3.8e-05) and not with depth (p = 0.93). Ranked within each mouse and tested by permuting within mice, which removes differences between mice and the dependence of relative latency on a mouse's number of fibers, the gradient remains (r = -0.223, p = 0.0014).

Tone relative latency: tail median 308 ms (n 32), anterior median 368 ms (n 164)

Result: reproduced. Over the 196 fibers with a tone latency (the earlier of increase and decrease), relative latency is shorter posteriorly (rho(AP, latency) = 0.254, p = 0.00033; tail median 308 ms against 368 ms anterior). Taken separately, neither increases (rho = -0.07, p = 0.5) nor decreases (rho = -0.21, p = 0.028, the opposite sign) show this gradient, so it comes from the tail's fast increases and the anterior striatum's slower decreases, as the paper states for Figure S6A-B. Ranked within each mouse and tested by permuting within mice, the gradient remains (r = 0.214, p = 0.003).

Pairwise correlations of D1 SPN Ca2+ signals are generally low but variable, and drop off significantly with the distance between fiber tips.

Result: reproduced. Pairwise correlations of the 61 fibers are low (median r = 0.163, IQR -0.025 to 0.361) and variable (range -0.678 to 0.904), and fall with distance between tips (r = -0.190 across 1830 pairs, p = 2.8e-16; mean r 0.293 in the closest quarter of pairs against 0.133 in the farthest). The other session gives the same (r = -0.238). The p-value treats pairs as independent, as the code does.

Result: reproduced. In the paper's linear model, the distance between fibers on the bundle image has no effect once tip distances are included (coefficient -3.4e-05 per pixel, 95% CI -2.7e-04 to 2.0e-04, p = 0.77), while tip distance does (Euclidean coefficient -0.278, p < 1e-5). The other session gives p = 0.41. Fibers adjacent on the bundle correlate slightly more (0.222 against 0.156), which the model attributes to their tips also being closer (bundle and tip distances correlate at r = 0.437).

fig1d-chronic-reward-stability¶

Dopamine release to unpredicted water reward is reliable and of comparable amplitude over at least 12 weeks after implantation (median over 44 fibers, normalized to week 5).

In [26]:
first = min(pd.Timestamp(s["start"]) for s in D15)


def weekly(sessions):
    rows = []
    for s in sessions:
        if len(s["act"]):
            wk = 5 + (pd.Timestamp(s["start"]) - first).days // 7
            rows.append((wk, s["act"]))
    weeks = sorted({w for w, _ in rows})
    means = {w: np.concatenate([a for ww, a in rows if ww == w]).mean(0) for w in weeks}
    counts = {w: sum(len(a) for ww, a in rows if ww == w) for w in weeks}
    init = means[weeks[0]][:31].max(0)
    tab = pd.DataFrame([{"week": w, "rewards": counts[w], "median": np.median(means[w][:31].max(0) / init),
                         "q25": np.percentile(means[w][:31].max(0) / init, 25), "q75": np.percentile(means[w][:31].max(0) / init, 75),
                         "median peak dff": np.median(means[w][:31].max(0))} for w in weeks])
    return tab


main = weekly([s for s in D15 if s["n_rew"] <= 25])

ax.errorbar(allr.week + 0.1, allr["median"], yerr=[allr["median"] - allr.q25, allr.q75 - allr["median"]], fmt="s--", c="0.5", label="all rewards")

def counts(sessions, inc_mask):
    good_stim, responders = [], set()
    for o in sessions:
        sig = o["resp"]["sig"] & inc_mask
        others = sig.copy()
        others[o["stim"]] = False
        if others.sum() >= 1:
            good_stim.append(o)
        responders |= set(np.flatnonzero(sig))
    return good_stim, responders

      f" ({len(good) / len(stim_inc):.2f}; paper 18 of 24, 0.75)")
print(f"Included recording locations with a significant response to at least one stimulation: {len(responders)} of {int(inc.sum())}")
resp_other = set()
for o in stim_inc:
    s_ = o["resp"]["sig"] & inc
    s_[o["stim"]] = False
    resp_other |= set(np.flatnonzero(s_))
print(f"Variant, counting only responses to another fiber's stimulation: {len(resp_other)} of {int(inc.sum())}"
      f" (dropped: {sorted(r + 1 for r in responders - resp_other)})")

                     "sig up others": int((o["resp"]["sig_up"] & inc).sum() - o["resp"]["sig_up"][o["stim"]]),
                     "sig any others": int((o["resp"]["sig"] & inc).sum() - o["resp"]["sig"][o["stim"]]),
                     "stim fiber sig": bool(o["resp"]["sig"][o["stim"]])} for o in stim_inc]).to_string(index=False))
# Variant: the code's further exclusions (fibers 8, 9 of 35 um and broken fiber 21; 1-based)
inc_code = inc.copy()
inc_code[[7, 8, 20]] = False
good_c, resp_c = counts([o for o in stim_inc if inc_code[o["stim"]]], inc_code)
print(f"\nVariant, code's exclusions: locations {int(inc_code.sum())}; stimulated with a response elsewhere {len(good_c)} of"
      f" {len([o for o in stim_inc if inc_code[o['stim']]])}; responding recording locations {len(resp_c)}")
# Variant: fibers labelled striatal but not included (candidates for "on the border")
tabO = o2[0]["table"]
striatal = tabO.location.isin(["Caudoputamen", "Striatum", "Nucleus accumbens"]).values
inc_b = inc | striatal

stim_b = [o for o in o2 if inc_b[o["stim"]]]

Result: partially reproduced. 22 Opto2 fibers are flagged included (expected 24 +- 2.4), and 20 of them respond to at least one stimulation (expected 22 +- 2.2), both within tolerance; 14 of the 19 stimulated included fibers evoke a significant response at another included fiber, below the expected 18 +- 1.8. As a fraction, 14 of 19 (0.74) is close to the paper's 18 of 24 (0.75); the denominators differ because fewer included fibers were stimulated in the files. Counting only responses to another fiber's stimulation, so that a stimulated fiber's own photoswitching does not count, still gives 20 responding locations. Counting the two fibers labelled Caudoputamen but not flagged (16 and 34) gives exactly the paper's 24 locations and 22 responding ones, and 16 of 21 stimulated fibers with a response elsewhere; the files hold 29 single-fiber sessions, of which only 21 stimulate a striatal fiber, so 18 of 24 cannot be reached. The included flag appears to mark fibers within the striatum, not those on its border.

fig6gh-release-decays-with-distance¶

Stimulating dopamine axons through one fiber evokes release at neighbouring non-stimulated sites that drops off sharply with distance in all three dimensions.

Result: reproduced. Over 266 pairs of 14 stimulated and 20 recording fibers (the paper has 378, 18 by 21), the response falls with distance as a = 0.0147 DF/F, b = -1.096 per mm (95% bootstrap interval -1.325 to -0.890), and with the absolute distance along each axis (Spearman rho -0.30 ML, -0.27 AP, -0.39 DV; all p < 1e-5). The binned mean falls from 0.0079 DF/F at 0.54 mm to 0.0013 to 0.0017 beyond 2 mm, and significant responses lie closer (median 0.95 mm) than the others (1.57 mm).

fig6g-dorsal-spread¶

Evoked release drops off less with distance dorsal to the stimulated fiber than ventral to it, consistent with dorsally extending dopamine axon branches.

In [29]:
def two_rates(df):
    out = {}
    for name, m in (("dorsal", df.dDV < 0), ("ventral", df.dDV > 0)):
        out[name] = V.exp_fit(df.dist[m].values, df.resp[m].values)[1]
    return out


rates = two_rates(P6)
print(f"dorsal sites {int((P6.dDV < 0).sum())}, ventral sites {int((P6.dDV > 0).sum())}")
print(f"decay rate b: dorsal {rates['dorsal']:.3f}, ventral {rates['ventral']:.3f} per mm")
diffs = []
for _ in range(1000):
    pick = rng_fit.choice(sites, len(sites), replace=True)
    sub = pd.concat([P6[P6.stim == s] for s in pick])
    try:
        rr = two_rates(sub)
        diffs.append(rr["dorsal"] - rr["ventral"])
    except RuntimeError:
        diffs.append(np.nan)
diffs = np.array(diffs)
print(f"difference dorsal - ventral {rates['dorsal'] - rates['ventral']:.3f}; 95% bootstrap interval {np.nanpercentile(diffs, 2.5):.3f}"
      f" to {np.nanpercentile(diffs, 97.5):.3f} (failed {int(np.isnan(diffs).sum())})")
for name, m in (("dorsal", P6.dDV < 0), ("ventral", P6.dDV > 0)):
    rho, p = stats.spearmanr(P6.dDV[m].abs(), P6.resp[m])
    print(f"{name}: Spearman rho(|dDV|, response) = {rho:.3f}, p = {p:.2g}; mean response {P6.resp[m].mean():.4f}")

fig6-tdtomato-control-no-response¶

In control mice expressing tdTomato in place of rDAm3.0, single-fiber stimulation evokes no significant fluorescence increase at non-stimulated sites (0 of 48 sites, 26 stimulations in 2 mice), so the release is not a hemodynamic effect.

Result: reproduced. In the tdTomato mice no included non-stimulated fiber shows a significant increase after stimulation: 0 of 304 fiber and session pairs in Opto4 (13 sessions) and 0 of 203 in Opto9 (12 sessions), with median responses of -0.0002 and 0.0003 DF/F; one Opto9 pair has a significant decrease. The same test finds increases in 142 of 619 pairs (20 distinct fibers) in Opto2. The files hold 25 tdTomato sessions where the paper reports 26 stimulations. The stimulated fiber is taken as the one with the largest laser artefact, which can be wrong when the artefact spreads; the true stimulated fiber is then among those tested, which makes the test stricter.

The paper also required these sites to respond to reward; UG21 has no reward events in the files (data check), so that inclusion step cannot be applied.

Claims not tested here¶

The data of these claims are not in the dandiset. Except for Figure S3, the paper deposited them on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.10272874); this attempt did not test them there.

  • figs1-no-tissue-damage: NeuN and DAPI images of implanted and unimplanted striatum (SuppFig01.zip).
  • figs3-targeting-errors: the dandiset's fiber table holds the localized tips but no planned targets (data check). The paper's code (SuppFig03/B/analysis_code/planned_v_actual.m) reads the planned targets from per-mouse calibration files (calibPath), which are in none of the Zenodo archives; SuppFig03.zip holds only the CT fiber tables (MATLAB table objects) and the code. Blocked as data_missing.
  • fig3-freely-moving-signals: miniscope recordings in freely moving mice (Fig03.zip).
  • fig7d-ventral-not-dorsal-jaw and fig7ef-single-ventral-fiber: the D1-cre mice OptoD1_6, 7, 8 and 10, their DeepLabCut jaw tracking and stimulation files (Fig07.zip, SuppFig07.zip). None of these mice is in the dandiset.

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The GLM, its null and the latency rule follow the Methods and the paper's code, re-implemented in Python: the low-pass filter is a Butterworth filter in place of MATLAB's lowpass; the locomotion lags come from a cross-correlation that shifts negative lags, where the code does not (the code's version is shown, r = 0.997 for light and 0.989 for tone with the main values); latencies are counted from the onset frame as in the Methods, where the code counts one frame later. DL18's tones include all 44 presentations, as the files do not give their frequency (its 14 12-kHz tones are used as a variant). Stimulation times and stimulated fibers in the optogenetic sessions are found from the DF/F alone, without the trigger line. The striatal tail boundary (-1.0 mm) and several criteria (thresholds for "many", "low", "comparable") are choices made here, before the analysis. The pooled spatial correlations are also shown ranked within mice; the figs4eh splits with a pre-onset baseline; the figs5 GLM with 13 spline functions. The test's chance rate per fiber (0.024 for an increase) is far from the paper's stated p < 1e-6, which assumes independent frames.

What was found about the dandiset. It holds the data of Figures 1C-D, 4, 5, 6, S2D-F, S4, S5E-H, S6 and S7A, and for the 7 salient-stimulus mice the traces, fiber order and stimulus times are exactly those of the paper's analysis. This match was not checked for DL15, 842, DL31, DL32 or the optogenetic mice. Missing are: the stimulation times and the identity of the stimulated fiber in every optogenetic session; the frequency of DL18's tones; the planned fiber targets of Figure S3 (not public); the task variables that separate unpredicted rewards in DL15's later sessions; one tdTomato session; the data of Figures 2, 3, 7, S1 and S5A-D (on Zenodo). The included column is described as "successfully implanted" but marks fibers within the striatum, leaving out border fibers the optogenetic analysis counts; UG21's indicator is given as tdTomato where the paper's counts and code identify it as the rDAm3.0 mouse without opsin; the archive's summary gives the approach as cell population imaging; and the DL31 and DL32 series store a regular frame rate whose times drift by up to half a second from the frame timestamps of the behaviour.
